\begin{proof}
The set $S_{\Omega}$ of all permutations of $\Omega$ is a group under composition. For every $n\in\Omega$ with $n\ge 2$, let $\tau_n$ be the transposition that swaps $1$ and $n$ and fixes all other elements. The elements $\tau_n$ are pairwise distinct, because $\tau_n(n)=1$, whereas for $m\ne n$ with $m\ge2$, $\tau_m(n)=n$. Therefore the map
\[
\{n\in\Omega:n\ge2\}\longrightarrow S_{\Omega},\qquad n\longmapsto\tau_n,
\]
is injective. Its domain is infinite, so $S_{\Omega}$ is infinite. Hence $S_{\Omega}$ is an infinite group.
\end{proof}

\[
\tau_n(1)=n,\qquad \tau_n(n)=1,\qquad \tau_n(k)=k\quad(k\notin\{1,n\}).
\]
Thus $\tau_n$ is the transposition $(1\ n)$ and belongs to $S_{\Omega}$. If $m,n\ge2$ and $m\ne n$, then $\tau_n(1)=n\ne m=\tau_m(1)$, so $\tau_n\ne\tau_m$. Consequently, $S_{\Omega}$ contains the infinite set $\{\tau_n:n\ge2\}$. Since permutations form a group under composition, $S_{\Omega}$ is an infinite group.
\end{proof}
